svg.title: Spatial disorientation and vestibular illusions
svg.desc: The three orientation systems, vestibular, somatosensory and visual, with a simple drawing of the three semicircular canals. A table of vestibular illusions: the leans, coriolis, graveyard spiral, somatogravic, inversion and elevator, with the cause of each and the likely pilot reaction. Also the visual illusions false horizon and autokinesis, and coping advice: trust the instruments.
svg.text: Spatial disorientation: where it comes from
Three semicircular canals at
right angles: roll, pitch, yaw
Vestibular system: organs of the inner ear sense position by balance. Each
canal is fluid-filled with fine hairs; acceleration bends the hairs and sends
nerve impulses to the brain.
Somatosensory system: nerves in skin, muscles and joints sense position from
gravity, feeling and sound ("seat of the pants"). It cannot tell gravity from
maneuvering forces.
Visual system: the eyes. In VMC the eyes usually win over false sensations; in
IMC, with visual cues removed, a pilot can quickly become disoriented.
Vestibular illusions: what the body feels, what the pilot may do
Illusion
Cause
Likely pilot reaction
The leans
Sudden return to level after a gradual, unnoticed
turn (2 degrees/second or less is below
detection).
Feels banked the other way; leans toward
the original turn.
Coriolis
Head moves in another plane while in a long turn,
as when looking at something in the flight deck.
Feels a turn or acceleration on a
different axis; may maneuver into a
dangerous attitude.
Graveyard spiral
Long, coordinated, constant-rate turn feels like
no turn; leveling feels like a turn the other
way.
Returns to the original turn, then pulls
back to stop a felt level descent. This
tightens the spiral and loses altitude.
Somatogravic
Rapid acceleration (takeoff) feels like tilting
the head back: nose-up.
Pushes nose low or dives. Rapid
deceleration does the opposite: pulls nose
up toward a stall.
Inversion
Abrupt change from climb to straight and level
feels like tumbling backward.
Pushes abruptly nose low, which can
intensify it.
Elevator
Abrupt upward acceleration (updraft) feels like a
climb.
Pushes nose low. A downdraft has the
opposite effect: pulls nose up.
Visual illusions (the eyes alone)
False horizon: sloping clouds, obscured horizon,
aurora, ground lights and stars. The pilot may
align with it and fly a dangerous attitude.
Autokinesis: in the dark a stationary light
stared at seems to move. The pilot may chase it
and lose control.
Coping (from the text)
Trust the instruments and disregard sensory
perceptions.
Avoid sudden head movement, especially on
takeoffs, turns and approaches.
Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, sleep loss
and mild hypoxia raise susceptibility.
